claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles are intrinsically structurally unstable at elevated temperatures.
In HENA nanoparticles, surface-energy effects dominate configurational-entropy stabilization.
Surface-energy dominance accelerates atomic diffusion, phase separation, and grain growth in HENA nanoparticles.
Nanoscale HENA behavior deviates from that of bulk HENAs.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles with grains below 10 nm can initially exhibit a single-phase FCC or BCC structure at room temperature.
Surface-energy-driven diffusion and chemical short-range-order evolution facilitate phase separation and grain coarsening.
High surface energy can promote structural phase transformation in metallic nanostructures.
High surface energy reduces the effective activation barrier for atomic diffusion in HENA nanoparticles.
Bulk high-entropy alloys exhibit a sluggish or hysteresis diffusion effect.
The nanoparticle surface effect counteracts sluggish diffusion and accelerates elemental segregation into lower-energy phases.
Surface-area minimization and phase separation reduce the total free energy and drive grain growth.
Annealing at 700 K will cause rapid loss of single-phase stability and formation of secondary phases in these nanoparticles.
Annealing at 700 K will produce grain growth beyond 50 nm within hours.
This structural evolution will degrade the mechanical and thermal properties of the nanoparticles.
Bulk HENAs possess high microstructural and thermal stability.
Bulk HENAs remain single-phase and fine-grained up to 1000 K because of configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and sluggish diffusion.

High-entropy alloys depart from traditional alloy design based primarily on mixing enthalpy by using multiple principal elements and associated high-entropy, lattice-distortion, diffusion, and cocktail effects.
Nanoparticles larger than 50 nm behave sufficiently like bulk material that the proposed instability mechanism fails.
Strong negative mixing enthalpies favor ordered phases and place the composition outside the proposed model's validity.
Experimental finite-temperature information for single-phase high-entropy alloys is limited.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify ambient pressure while simultaneously describing vacuum as an ambient-pressure environment; vacuum and ambient pressure are not equivalent boundary conditions.
